ideaPoints: White gives up his well-posted knight on c5 for Black's passive, theoretically 'bad' bishop on d7: a deliberate transformation of one kind of advantage into another rather than a win of material.
After the trade White is left with a light-squared bishop against a knight, the kind of position Fischer valued and handled best; the plan is to press Black with that bishop.
Black was preparing to exchange rooks on the open a-file and then contest it with ...Ra8; the bishop on a7 plugs the file and prevents that exchange (prophylaxis).
Behind the bishop White can double his own rooks on the a-file at leisure, keeping control of the file for himself.
Black is left without a plan and is helpless while White gradually improves his position (a 'stranglehold').
The knight on c3 was White's one badly placed piece: it had no squares because b5 and d5 are covered by the c6-pawn (and it is hemmed in by its own e4 and a4 pawns), so it is rerouted.
From b1 the knight heads for d2, from where it can join the game via c4 or via f3 (to g5), adding to the pressure on f7.
The retreat also clears the way for c2-c3, driving away Black's active knight on b4, and uncovers the queen's defence of c2 (answering the idea ...Rxd2 and ...Nxc2).
If Black exchanges rooks on d2, the recapture Nxd2 simply helps the knight on its way.
The knight establishes itself on d3, deep in White's position, where it is extremely powerful and hard to dislodge.
Together with the bishop on f5, the d3-knight paralyses all three of White's major pieces (Kasparov's own assessment).
White's minor pieces are scattered on both flanks and cannot coordinate; the placement of his knights is especially poor.
White deliberately lets pawns go (c3 falls with check, then f4) in order to bring his king up the board: king activity matters more than material in this rook ending.
The target is the set-up king f6, pawn g6, rook h7, after which Black's pawns fall of their own accord (Alekhine).
Capablanca stops caring about material equality and thinks only of supporting his passed g-pawn (Reti).
Black offers the exchange (rook for bishop) in a position where there are no open files for the rooks to exploit.
Moving the rook off e7 frees that square for the knight, which can then go via e7 to a strong outpost on d5.
From d5 the knight attacks the c3-pawn, and White's bishop on b2 is of little use unless it relocates to d2.
Black's blockade on the light squares then becomes practically impossible to break.
White voluntarily accepts a permanently backward e-pawn and gives up control of e5, a concession that looks like a beginner's error.
In return the advance cramps Black's position.
White gains the e6 square as an outpost for a knight and opens the h2-b8 diagonal for his bishop.
Described as the key move of the game: it strikes at Black's pawn centre (c5/d5/e6) at once and leaves Black without a good reply.
After Black's answer 20...d4 his central pawns have no hope of advancing further, while White's bishop is unimpeded (it soon took up the a2-g8 diagonal).
With the centre fixed White gets a free hand for a kingside pawn advance (f4, e5, later f5) and steadily gains momentum.
The move looks anti-positional: it invites Bxh5, which shatters Black's kingside pawn structure (doubled, isolated h-pawns).
Fischer judged that the kingside activity Black obtains in return gives significant counterplay, and that judgement proved correct in the game.
White had achieved nothing concrete and Black's pressure on d4 should hold the balance; the piece not earning its keep is the knight on c3.
The dream square for the knight is d6, and the retreat starts the route b1-a3-c4-d6.
Once the knight reaches d6 it is transformed from White's worst piece into a monster that changes the whole evaluation.
Black's last move (12...Qd7) finally broke the pin on the f6-knight and prepared ...Nh7 and ...f5; 13.g4 is aimed squarely at denying that kingside play.
White already has more space in the centre and is preparing b2-b4 on the queenside; if he also takes space on the kingside he is master of the whole board.
It is prophylaxis as a strategy: on the plan ...Nh7 and ...Bf6 (to trade or activate the bad g7-bishop) Petrosian intended Bg3 and h4, stopping that too.
alternativePoints: Castling was the move most players would have chosen and would have left White with a good position.
But it does nothing to prevent ...Nh7 and ...f5, so Black would get the kingside counterplay that Petrosian wanted to rule out completely.

ideaPoints: Before opening the queenside White first improves a piece: the bishop returns to h4 to attack the e7-knight and tie Black down.
Black has no active play at all, so there is no hurry; White can make the b4 break on his own terms a move later (24.b4 was played).
It illustrates Petrosian's principle of depriving the opponent of every scrap of counterplay before starting his own action.
alternativePoints: 23.b4 was the thematic break and Petrosian knew it, but it allows 23...f5! with sharp complications (24.bxc5 f4).
Even though those complications favour White, Petrosian saw no reason to give Black any hope when he could prepare b4 and play it without allowing them.

ideaPoints: Black's 26...a5 sought counterplay by prying open both the a- and b-files; Karpov's reasoning was that one open file can be contained but two cannot, so the second must be prevented.
After 27.a4 only the b-file opens, and White covers every entry square on it (b1-b4 with Bc3, Bd1, Nd2), so the file leads nowhere for Black's rooks.
The a5-pawn becomes a fixed target for the bishop on c3.
With the queenside sealed, White is free to pursue his light-square bind and breakthrough on the kingside.

White gives up his bishop for the e4-knight in order to change the minor-piece balance: if the e5-knights are also exchanged he is left with a strong knight against Black's very bad light-squared bishop.
After 14...fxe4 White follows with f2-f3, ripping open the e-file against the backward e6-pawn.
The result is a lasting bind: better minor pieces, more space and e-file pressure, which White later extends to the dark squares all over the board (e5, f6, h6).

The advance closes the queenside and takes away Black's remaining options there (the ...c5 break was already stopped by b4, and ...dxc4 is now ruled out too), so Black has trouble finding anything to do.
White has the better bishop and more space; the side with more space benefits from a closed position with few exchanges (the knight had just retreated with 19.Nf3 to avoid a trade).
With the queenside fixed White can go on to seize space on the kingside as well (g4, g5, h4-h5), leaving Black to wait passively until a breakthrough is prepared.

Black's only real asset is the better bishop: his queenside pawns stand on dark squares while White's stand (or can be forced) on light squares, where they block White's bishop and can be attacked by Black's.
Black keeps the queens on and centralises his own on e5, where it eyes the whole board, so that his two active pieces outclass White's.
The plan is then to probe so that White has to put more pawns on light squares (c4, g4 followed in the game), making his bishop steadily worse.
Queens are to be exchanged only once the resulting bishop ending has become winning, which is what eventually happened.
alternativePoints: Trading queens at once leads to a bishop ending White can hold: after 32.Kxf2 Kf7 33.Bd3 Kf6 34.c4 Ke5 35.Ke3 the black king cannot penetrate.
White would also have no clear weaknesses for Black to attack, so the small advantage of the better bishop could not be increased.

ideaPoints: Black has just forced the exchange of dark-squared bishops, leaving a dominant knight on c5 against a light-squared bishop hemmed in by its own pawns.
23...b6 takes Black's pawn off a light square, so the bishop has nothing to attack on the queenside.
It also prevents White's b5-b6, which would have loosened the d6-pawn and might have given the bishop the f1-a6 diagonal.
The bishop is thus entombed for good; even if it later reaches the h3-c8 diagonal it bites on nothing because Black's queenside pawns are on dark squares.
Pawns are equal on both wings and White's asset is the bishop pair; Black intended ...Rd8 followed by ...Nd4.
The retreat prepares c2-c3, which restricts the c6-knight and takes away the d4 square it was heading for.
From b1 the knight will re-emerge via d2 to c4, where it supports White's queenside pawn advance.
alternativePoints: Retreating to e2 is rejected because the knight belongs on c4, where it supports the queenside pawn advance; b1 (then d2) is the route to that square, e2 is not.

ideaPoints: Black's d5 and b5 squares are very weak and White also has the bishop pair; the question is how to convert these advantages.
The knight goes backwards in order to travel d2-b1-c3, from where it bears down on exactly those weak squares.
White does not recapture on h4 but sacrifices the pawn for a move, so that after 47...hxg3+ 48.Kxg3 the kingside is opened for his king.
The king then has two entry squares, f4 and h4, and marches in (Kg4-h5-g6) to attack Black's pawns.
It is a good-knight-versus-bad-bishop ending: Black's pawns are fixed on light squares (46.b4 fixed the queenside), so the knight has targets everywhere and the bishop has none.
alternativePoints: The natural recapture 47.gxh4 leaves a white pawn on h4 that blocks his own king's path forward.
Keeping the material would therefore cost White his king's route into Black's position, which is what the win depends on.

ideaPoints: The queen begins the manoeuvre d7-f5-h7, spending three tempi and ignoring ordinary development in order to put the queen on h7.
In Nimzowitsch's own words the whole idea of the queen manoeuvre is to restrain White's kingside pawns.
Restraint is not passive: Nimzowitsch calls every restraining action the logical prelude to an attack, and Black later follows with ...Nf5-h6, ...Rg8 and ...g5 to attack on the same wing.
White has given up his pawn centre (dxc5, then the e5-pawn was exchanged) and replaced it with pieces: the bishop on e5 is a blockader that stops Black's e6/d5 pawns from advancing.
13.Nd2 brings the knight towards f3 to reinforce the blockading force, so that d4 and e5 stay under White's control.
The aim is to keep the freeing break ...e6-e5 impossible, which leaves Black's pawns immobile and his pieces (notably the d7-bishop) shut in; the central grip later becomes a kingside attack.
alternativePoints: 13.Qc2 goes after the h7-pawn, but after 13...O-O 14.Bxf6 Rxf6 15.Bxh7+ Kh8 16.Bg6 Black plays 16...e5!.
White has won a pawn but given up the blockade: Black gets a mobile pawn centre and very active pieces, which is worth more than the pawn.

ideaPoints: White is slightly worse: a5 is weak and Black controls the d-file. Rather than tie his pieces to the a-pawn, Carlsen lets it go in return for active play.
After 28...Nbxa5 Black's extra pawn costs him coordination: a knight is stuck on the edge of the board and his pieces are tied to defending a6.
White follows with 29.Ne3, keeping pieces on, so it is Black who has to work to untangle; objectively the game is about equal but White now has the easier play.
alternativePoints: Defending the pawn with 28.Rea1 lets Black improve freely (...Nd6, ...Nd4, ...g5) and leaves White with no counterplay.
Passive defence would keep material level but give White a position in which he can only wait.

ideaPoints: Black declines to exchange light-squared bishops and retreats instead, keeping more tension in the position.
The position then resembles a King's Indian: Black attacks on the kingside (...f4, ...g5-g4), and White must find queenside play, which is harder to conduct.
